title: Lakshmana follows
carry: seva: serving is a way to love god

lines: I'LL KEEP WATCH WHILE YOU SLEEP.
cards: Nobody asked Lakshmana to go. Nobody exiled him. He could stay in the palace for fourteen years, a prince, with his own wife, Urmila, and a comfortable life.
Rama even tells him to stay: look after our mothers, look after the kingdom. Lakshmana falls at his brother's feet and says no.

The two have been inseparable since they were boys; the text says Rama couldn't sleep unless Lakshmana was beside him, couldn't eat unless he ate too. So Lakshmana says: I'll go ahead of you with a bow.
I'll dig for roots and gather fruit. I'll keep watch while you and Sita sleep. Just don't leave me here.

teach.h: THINK OF THE FOREST AS AYODHYA.
teach.b: Then Lakshmana goes to say goodbye to his own mother, Sumitra, and she blesses him. In Valmiki's words, roughly: think of Rama as your father, Dasharatha. Think of Sita as me, your mother.
Think of the forest as Ayodhya, your home. Now go, my son. Home is wherever these people are.
Hindus have a word for what Lakshmana does: seva, service.
Not service for pay, but service as love, and here, service to God, since Rama is Vishnu born human. Lakshmana carries the bags, builds the hut, stays awake.

That's why, in the Ram darbar, the picture of Rama's court in many Hindu homes and temples, Lakshmana stands right beside Rama and Sita, and Hanuman kneels at their feet: two great servants, honored next to God.
In temples today, people still do seva: sweeping, cooking, serving food, handing out prasad. The story is honest about the cost, too.
Lakshmana leaves his wife, Urmila, behind for fourteen years, and Valmiki says almost nothing about her.
Later tellings filled the silence: in one well-known folk version, she sleeps for fourteen years so her husband can stay awake.
Now look back at this week. God came down as a baby. Even Rama walked behind a guru.
A garland put Sita's name first.
A king kept a word that broke him. A prince accepted his dharma in one breath. A wife claimed her share of it.
And a brother nobody asked, went anyway, to serve.

how: In many Hindu temples and home shrines, Rama is shown with Sita on one side and Lakshmana on the other, often with Hanuman kneeling before them; Lakshmana is honored as the model of a devoted brother.

o: Rama's brother chooses exile though no one asked
the king orders Rama's brother to guard him
Rama's brother stays home to guard the kingdom

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: think of the forest as Ayodhya

s: Lakshmana was exiled along with Rama
nobody exiled him. he chose to go.
Valmiki tells Urmila's story in detail
the old text says almost nothing about her; later tellings filled the silence.
Sumitra tells Lakshmana to think of Sita as his mother
and Rama as his father, and the forest as home.

games.q: you're Lakshmana. your brother is going into exile and asks you to stay home and look after everyone. what do you do?
o: fall at his feet and insist on going.
go later, once the palace is settled.
games.why: he refuses to stay and goes as their guard. his mother blesses it: the forest will be his Ayodhya.

practice: Plan one small seva for today, without being asked and without telling anyone: wash someone's dishes, carry someone's bags, help at your temple.
If you pray, offer it to God, the way Lakshmana served Rama; if you don't, offer it to the person. And spare a thought for the Urmilas, the people who stay behind so someone else can go.

wordCard.voice: Lakshmana follows. Rama's brother goes into exile unasked, with his mother's blessing: the forest will be your home.

orig.note: Sanskrit: marked with good signs, or fortunate; Rama's brother.

carryVoice: Your line: seva, serving is a way to love God. The one who stays awake so the others can sleep. Day forty-two, and a week of the Ramayana.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 18 (Rama and Lakshmana inseparable from childhood)
Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 31 (Lakshmana insists on going)
